items.name: Readability
items.evidence: All code is inline `python3 -c` one-liners with single-letter names: `d=open(...)`, `c=sqlite3.connect(...)`, `r=[... for i,n,v in ...]`. There are no comments explaining the XOR key. The single-letter-name cap applies.

items.name: Maintainability
items.evidence: There is no re-runnable decrypt or extract script, only ad-hoc shell one-liners, against the convention asking for 'a small decrypt script'. Extraction queries a /tmp/w copy instead of /app. The scope is small and there is no dead code in /app.

items.name: Robustness
items.evidence: `b^0x42` is hardcoded with no explanation in code. The decrypted magic is not checked in code, though xxd was run manually afterwards. There is no error handling, but nothing is silently swallowed and errors would propagate.

items.name: Recovery method is principled
items.evidence: The key came from evidence: the WAL padding was all 0x42 ('BBBB'), i.e. XORed zero bytes. The agent decrypted the whole file, let SQLite replay the WAL, ran `pragma integrity_check` (ok), checked count(*)=11 on a fresh copy, and confirmed the header `377f 0682`.

items.name: Original evidence preserved before in-place repair
items.name_zh: 原地修复前保留原始文件
items.evidence: The first decrypt went to a /tmp/w copy. `cp main.db-wal /tmp/main.db-wal.orig` ran before the in-place overwrite, and the agent then confirmed /app/main.db-wal equals the XOR of the backup (`wal-ok`). main.db was left unmodified.
